subject: Species density by post stratify or sql

messages.author: 742dcce8e57130f3
messages.subject: Species density by post stratify or sql
parts:
Dear all,

I need some help with getting basic density and abundance estimates. 

I am working with data from 2009 where 38 points were systematically established and surveyed twice. There are only enough detection numbers for 4 or 5 species to be analyzed. I want to get density and abundance estimates for each species. I have tried two different ways to get the results; 1) specify which species in the SQL Where box and 2) Post-stratify by species. I get different results for each of these methods and I'm not sure which one is correct. For example; SQL method I get 412 REVI but Post-stratify method I get 641 REVI.

My other issue is that I get different density and abundance results depending on the number of total individuals in the dataset.
For example;
1)  I ran 6 species with 290 individuals. I analyzed Northern parula and got an abundance of 1,040. 
2) I ran 8 species with 306 individuals. I analyzed Northern parula again and got an abundance of 938. 
3) I ran all 28 species with 503 individuals. I analyzed Northern parula and got an abundance  of 5,440. 

Now my sample size for this species is lower than what is recommended (<60) so would that be the reason my estimates are all over the place? 

Thank you for your help,
Meredith

messages.author: 1fb54f491646a589
messages.subject: RE: [distance-sampling] Species density by post stratify or sql
parts:
Meredith, when you do a run with multiple species, you're assuming that individuals of all species are equally detectable.  For common species, you should analyse one species at a time.  For rarer species, you could analyse them with more common species that you expect to have similar detectability, but you should not pool data across species with very different detectabilities - unless you ask Distance to fit a different detection function within each stratum (species).

A better option is probably to use the mcds engine of Distance, and specify species as a factor-type covariate.  This fits a common model across species, but allowing the scale of the detection function to vary by species.  You might still want to split your species into groups, so that species with very different detectabilities are not analysed together.

Steve Buckland

parts:
Ok! This makes sense. I ran the multi-species data set through the mcds engine and used species as a covariate while also post-stratifying species which gave me detection probability. From there, I grouped species with similar detection probabilities and reran the mcds engine using groups as a covariate and again post-stratifying species. I want to clarify that although this changed the detection probabilities where grouped species had the same values, it provides more reliable density estimates since these values are extracting information from similar species. Do I understand this correctly?  

I now realize that others have asked this question in previous posts but the way the questions were worded, I had trouble figuring out how this applied to my data. Thank you for explaining it once again. 

Meredith
